title: Redwood discovery - Lyra MedTech latency & throughput
summary: Discovery call focused on p95 latency targets, concurrency and streaming behavior for Redwood hosted vs dedicated vs private deployments. Customer is Lyra MedTech (regulated healthcare) wants <200ms p95 for short chat prompts at 50 concurrent users and burst to 200, ask about prefix/KV caching, token/sec benchmarks, encryption/KMS, SOC2, VPC, and pilot/benchmarks. Next steps: share security docs, run a dedicated benchmark, send pricing and suggested config, schedule follow-up demo/benchmark window.
action_items: Jordan Kim - Send draft pricing/committed capacity options + Hosted vs Dedicated comparison - due 2026-04-23
Samir Patel - Share benchmark plan template and request list (prompt set, sample payloads, concurrency profile) - due 2026-04-22
Lina Gomez - Provide VPC peering/network constraints and IP allowlist window for pilot - due 2026-04-24
Michael Reyes - Share 20 sample prompts and 5 larger inference templates for token/sec tests - due 2026-04-22
next_steps: Redwood to run a dedicated benchmark (p95/report) using Lyra sample prompts
Redwood to share SOC 2 + security whitepaper and KMS integration docs
Schedule 60-min pilot kickoff and network setup call
Follow-up meeting to review benchmark results and recommended config
transcript:
[00:00] Jordan Kim: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Jordan from Redwood, AE on the account. Samir is our SE, he'll handle the perf questions. Quick intros?
[00:08] Dr. Aisha Khan: Hi, Aisha here, CTO at Lyra. We're trying to understand if Redwood can meet our latency SLAs for chat features in our clinician app.
[00:15] Michael Reyes: Mike, Head of ML, I'll own the benchmarks and integration.
[00:19] Lina Gomez: Lina, infra. I'll do networking and security.
[00:22] Samir Patel: Great, thanks. Quick agenda: scope p95 targets, concurrency, streaming behavior, and then discuss Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private for regulated data. Sound OK?
[00:32] Dr. Aisha Khan: Yes. Our target is roughly <200ms p95 for short prompt completions (like 15-40 tokens). We expect 50 concurrent active users during clinic hours with spikes to 200 for short windows. We also stream partial outputs to the UI.
[00:46] Jordan Kim: Understood. Can you tell us about model choices? Are you evaluating smaller open models or planning to use larger ones?
[00:53] Michael Reyes: We're leaning toward an LLaMA-derivative quantized model for on-prem, but will consider hosted variants for initial rollout. Quality matters; 15-40 token responses are common, but we also have some 200 token summaries.
[01:05] Samir Patel: Thanks. Two quick clarifications: when you say <200ms p95, is that observed token-to-first-token (streaming first byte) or full response completion?
[01:13] Dr. Aisha Khan: We care mainly about first token latency for UX, and overall completion p95 ideally under 500ms for the longer ones. So first byte p95 <200ms, completion p95 <500ms for under 200 tokens.
[01:25] Lina Gomez: From infra, we need VPC peering and KMS/HSM integration since PHI may be involved. SOC 2 and audit logs are mandatory.
[01:33] Jordan Kim: We support VPC/private deployments and KMS. We'll share the SOC 2 pack after the call.
[01:38] Samir Patel: For latency, we normally look at three levers: model size/quantization, batching/concurrency, and routing/caching. For streaming first-byte p95 at low token lengths, serving on Dedicated with pinned GPUs or a Private VPC deployment usually gives best predictability. Hosted can also meet targets depending on commit.
[01:54] Michael Reyes: Can you share typical token/sec numbers? We need to run a token/sec benchmark to project costs and concurrency.
[01:59] Samir Patel: Sure — rough numbers: on a rtx-6000/gen3 class GPU with optimized kernels and int8 quantization, you can get ~400-800 tokens/sec for generation workloads for these smaller prompts; with batching you can push aggregate throughput but latencies shift. For p95 under 200ms first-byte at 50 concurrent users, we typically recommend either Dedicated with capacity sized for steady-state or Hosted with reserved capacity.
[02:20] Dr. Aisha Khan: For streaming on mobile, jitter matters. How does Redwood handle prefix or KV cache to reduce repeated context compute?
[02:27] Samir Patel: We support prefix caching and KV cache reuse. If your prompts reuse similar context — patient history or system prompt — that dramatically reduces compute per request. Note: the transcript from our internal docs sometimes says K V cache and it's auto-transcribed oddly, but it's KV cache in the product.
[02:41] Jordan Kim: Can you describe the concurrency profile — are the 50 concurrent users sustained or more bursty?
[02:47] Michael Reyes: Sustained during clinic hours, but we see bursts up to 200 for 30-60 second windows around shift changes.
[02:55] Samir Patel: OK. For a burst to 200, we'd consider autoscaling/burst capacity on Dedicated or routing to hosted fallback tiers. Latency SLOs can be kept by pre-warming and allowing short-lived burst instances, but cost grows.
[03:08] Lina Gomez: About data residency — we'd prefer Private (VPC) for PHI until audit completes. How different is the performance between Private on-prem and Redwood Dedicated?
[03:17] Samir Patel: Performance is a mix of hardware and network. If you provision similar GPU classes on-prem with our runtime, we can match latency. The main diff is network egress and orchestration layer for autoscaling. Often Dedicated in a colocated cloud region gives fastest time-to-value; Private on-prem gives more control but needs ops.
[03:34] Dr. Aisha Khan: Any suggestions for p95 targets we should set realistically?
[03:38] Samir Patel: For short responses (<=40 tokens) and first-byte streaming: p95 ~120-220ms is achievable on tuned Dedicated/private setups. On hosted with reserved capacity you can be in that ballpark, but on-demand hosted often has larger variance. For completion p95 up to 200 tokens, expect 300-700ms depending on model.
[03:57] Michael Reyes: Good. We also need to measure token/sec under load for cost projection. Can you run a benchmark with our prompt set?
[04:04] Jordan Kim: Yes — Samir will coordinate. We'll need sample prompts, average token lengths, concurrency schedule and network topology.
[04:12] Samir Patel: For the benchmark plan, we'll run: a) single-user latency curves with streaming enabled, b) sustained concurrency at 50 for 30 minutes, c) burst test to 200 for 2 minutes, and d) token/sec aggregate measurement across setups (hosted reserved, dedicated pool, private). We'll provide a spreadsheet for results.
[04:31] Michael Reyes: Do you support endpoint-level SLOs and tracing so we can correlate backend latencies?
[04:36] Jordan Kim: Yes — Console has per-route latency, token cost, and tracing hooks. We'll show you dashboards in the follow-up demo.
[04:44] Lina Gomez: Network security: will you need inbound peering or can you do egress-only? We prefer egress-only with IP allowlist.
[04:51] Samir Patel: Egress-only is common but for Private VPC peering we can do peering. We'll document both options and the changes needed on your side.
[05:00] Dr. Aisha Khan: For encryption, KMS for key rotation is mandatory. Do you have HSM or customer-managed keys?
[05:06] Jordan Kim: We support customer-managed KMS in Dedicated and Private; hosted can integrate with some KMS providers — we'll share specifics.
[05:13] Michael Reyes: Any known gotchas for tokenization differences across model variants? We need consistency between local and hosted runs.
[05:19] Samir Patel: Yes; tokenization can vary across model forks. We recommend standardizing on a tokenization library and we can run the same tokenizer in the benchmark. Also note that quantization sometimes slightly changes token/sec performance and output shapes.
[05:32] Dr. Aisha Khan: What's the timeline if we decide to pilot? We need security review, pilot, and then production in Q3.
[05:39] Jordan Kim: Typical pilot can start within 2–4 weeks after network setup and NDAs; benchmarks take 1 week to run and analyze. For Q3 production, you'd want a Dedicated commitment by early Q2.
[05:50] Michael Reyes: Cost sensitivity — can you give an order-of-magnitude for token costs with Dedicated vs Hosted?
[05:56] Samir Patel: Ballpark: Dedicated reduces per-token compute cost by ~30–60% vs on-demand hosted depending on utilization and batching. We'll send a pricing sheet with examples.
[06:05] Lina Gomez: Please include the security pack and a sample contract for Dedicated.
[06:10] Jordan Kim: We'll attach those.
[06:13] Samir Patel: One thing we should clarify: streaming impacts token/sec numbers because you often can't batch across streaming-first-byte requests as effectively. For first-byte p95 you might need smaller micro-batches which lowers tokens/sec but improves latency.
[06:28] Michael Reyes: Makes sense. For our UX we prefer sub-200ms first token, so we accept some throughput tradeoff.
[06:34] Dr. Aisha Khan: Can you do a test run against our staging environment? We can open a peered VPC or provide a test corpus.
[06:41] Jordan Kim: Yes, staging peering is ideal. Samir will coordinate the IPs and security checklist.
[06:47] Samir Patel: I'll send the benchmark template and required payloads. Also note that for p95 reporting we measure end-to-end including network hops, not only server-side. If you want server-only we can provide both breakdowns.
[06:59] Lina Gomez: We'll want server-only numbers for SLA negotiation.
[07:03] Samir Patel: Noted. We'll include split metrics (client-side end-to-end and server-only).
[07:10] Michael Reyes: Do you have an example benchmark for similar customers (healthcare)?
[07:15] Jordan Kim: We recently ran a benchmark with a telemed customer — we'll share anonymized results and a spreadsheet.
[07:21] Dr. Aisha Khan: Great. Let's recap next steps.
[07:26] Jordan Kim: Recap: 1) Jordan to send pricing and SOC2/security pack; 2) Samir to send benchmark plan/spreadsheet and schedule test window; 3) Lyra to share prompts and network constraints; 4) follow-up meeting to review results.
[07:38] Michael Reyes: Sounds good. Thanks, everyone.
[07:40] Dr. Aisha Khan: Thank you.
[07:41] Jordan Kim: Thanks — we'll follow up with calendar invites and docs.
[07:45] [call ends]
